messages.author: eb9271bf7fdc714d
messages.subject: pointrange dodge
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have the data pasted below, and I would like to use geom_pointrange.
I the "mean" column is the center of the range, the upper.bound is
the ymax, the lower.bound is the ymin. For each risk category, I need
to draw 2 point-ranges, coloured according to the value on the
"Number" variable. In my current code, I the point-ranges overlap. I
would like to "dodge" them, so that they stay next to each other, but
so that we can clearly distinguish between the ranges for each
"Number" category. Unfortunately, the position="dodge" command does
not seem to work for geom_pointrange.

There must be a simple solution for my problem, but I can't seem to
find it right now. Any help would be much appreciated!

Best,

Vincent
-----------------------------------------------
Current command:
ggplot(dataforplot,aes(riskcategory,mean,colour=Number))
+geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lower.bound,ymax=upper.bound))

Data:

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: pointrange dodge
parts:
Hi:

A couple of prefatory comments:
(1) Text strings such as Low # of BITS without enclosing quotes lead to trouble,
      especially for people who use textConnection() to cut and paste data into the
      R console. Firstly, # is a comment indicator; secondly, R is going to try to read
      what you intend as a single character string as four, and complain about
      the mismatch between the number of variable names and the number of
      distinct fields it read. (Fortunately, I saw that coming; others may not have.)
(2) In a ggplot() command, you want the + to be at the end of a line rather than at
     the beginning if you intend the second line of code to be a continuation of the first;
     otherwise, ggplot2 interprets the first line as a complete statement
     and tries to parse it.
More comments on this below.

I ended up copying and pasting the data to a file and editing the Number category
before entering it into R. In the end, I went with Low and High as the Number.

Since riskcategory is integer rather than a factor, the simplest way to generate a
'dodge' is to add a small amount to the riskcategory corresponding to High in the Number
factor; I used 0.2. More specifically,

dataforplot$riskcategory <- dataforplot$riskcategory + rep(c(0, 0.2), each = 6))
p <- ggplot(dataforplot,aes(riskcategory,mean,colour=Number))
p + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lower.bound,ymax=upper.bound))

gives you the dodged CIs by riskcategory colored by Number, with Number as the
title of the legend. If you prefer "# of BITS" as the legend title, then use
p + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lower.bound,ymax=upper.bound)) +
      scale_colour_hue("# of BITS")

Since I complained about the data format supplied, it's only fair that I show you
a better way to help people help you, and that is to use dput() on your data frame:

dput(dataforplot)
structure(list(riskcategory = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1.2, 2.2, 3.2,
4.2, 5.2, 6.2), mean = c(0.26, 0.27, 0.28, 0.17, 0.01, 0, 0.44,
0.27, 0.2, 0.09, 0, 0), sd = c(0.13, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.01, 0,
0.19, 0.1, 0.1, 0.08, 0.01, 0), lower.bound = c(0.063, 0.122,
0.112, 0.0275, 0.000151, 7.14e-07, 0.101, 0.104, 0.0395, 0.00448,
7.51e-06, 1.26e-08), upper.bound = c(0.54, 0.5, 0.49, 0.41, 0.04,
0.01, 0.79, 0.49, 0.43, 0.33, 0.03, 0), Number = structure(c(2L,
2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("High",
"Low"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("riskcategory", "mean",
"sd", "lower.bound", "upper.bound", "Number"), row.names = c(NA,
-12L), class = "data.frame")

It's even more helpful if you type in the name of your data object and then copy the
dput output to it when copying it into your e-mail, e.g.,

dataforplot <-  structure(list(riskcategory = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1.2, 2.2, 3.2,
4.2, 5.2, 6.2), mean = c(0.26, 0.27, 0.28, 0.17, 0.01, 0, 0.44,
0.27, 0.2, 0.09, 0, 0), sd = c(0.13, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.01, 0,
0.19, 0.1, 0.1, 0.08, 0.01, 0), lower.bound = c(0.063, 0.122,
0.112, 0.0275, 0.000151, 7.14e-07, 0.101, 0.104, 0.0395, 0.00448,
7.51e-06, 1.26e-08), upper.bound = c(0.54, 0.5, 0.49, 0.41, 0.04,
0.01, 0.79, 0.49, 0.43, 0.33, 0.03, 0), Number = structure(c(2L,
2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("High",
"Low"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("riskcategory", "mean",
"sd", "lower.bound", "upper.bound", "Number"), row.names = c(NA,
-12L), class = "data.frame")

Why does this matter? Because this way (a) it's a simple copy-and-paste
operation, and (b) the members of the list get the data in the form
you were using when the error in question occurred, which is not
necessarily the form that would be received when you copy the data object into
an e-mail verbatim. In your case, it's entirely possible that you set riskcategory to be a
factor, but when I read it into R from your mail, it was read as integer, so it was
trivial to generate the dodge effect. It may not have been quite as simple for
you if your copy of dataforplot had riskcategory as a factor, as an extra step
or two would have been required for the conversion.

Thank you for providing this example, as it presents an opportunity to explain
how to better provide data to the list when requesting help.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: pointrange dodge
parts:
If you do want to use position_dodge, you need to explicitly specify the width:

dataforplot$riskcategory <- round(dataforplot$riskcategory)
p <- ggplot(dataforplot,aes(riskcategory,mean,colour=Number))
p + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lower.bound,ymax=upper.bound), position =
position_dodge(width = 0.4))

Hadley

PS. Thanks Dennis for the reproducible example and explanation!

Thanks to Fernando, Dennis and Hadley for your replies. The solutions
your propose work perfectly, and I am extremely happy with the
resulting graph.

Of course, Dennis is right on all counts. I expected this to require a
trivial tweak of my ggplot command (Hadley's reply suggests this was
right), and I did not anticipate that people would need access to the
actual data. I will certainly remember to post dput, as well as
working code the next time I post to the list.

Again, thanks to all for your help. I really appreciate your work and efforts.

Best,

Vincent

On Mon, Apr 19, 2010 at 8:57 AM, Vincent Arel <vincen...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thanks to Fernando, Dennis and Hadley for your replies. The solutions
your propose work perfectly, and I am extremely happy with the
resulting graph.

That was the intention :)  Thanks to Hadley for clarifying the position_dodge option
in geom_pointrange. It didn't occur to me to check that (headslap) :-}

Of course, Dennis is right on all counts. I expected this to require a
trivial tweak of my ggplot command (Hadley's reply suggests this was
right), and I did not anticipate that people would need access to the
actual data. I will certainly remember to post dput, as well as
working code the next time I post to the list.

A point I want to emphasize about posting data with dput is that those inspired
to help have access to the data *in the form that the poster sees on his/her machine*.
This is critical: it is often the difference between a simple, effective, quick answer with
good feelings all around as opposed to a testy, contentious, drawn out exchange
over several hours or days that leaves the participants on both sides weary and frustrated.

The class mechanism in R can produce very subtle distinctions that inexperienced useRs
rarely appreciate until they get stung by them, usually when one wants output A but gets
output B (if any) because the R function expects an object of a certain class...or behaves differently
depending on the class of object it is presented. The nice thing about dput() is that a helper
has direct access to the data as the poster sees it and can more effectively test out
potential solutions or spot mistakes/flaws in the data or program that led to the error in a
much shorter time frame. If you lurk around R-help for a while, you'll find that people who
know how to help the helpers get more attention, get higher quality solutions and a greater
variety of solutions in very short order, often within minutes. That's neither an accident
nor a coincidence. (That's why the posting guide exists.)

I just felt it was time to stop exhorting/haranguing folks about posting data and code and just
show how it's done and why it's effective. It produced at least one convert (thanks, Vincent!!)
I also hope this inspires others and makes life a little easier for Hadley, too...

Best regards to all,
Dennis

Again, thanks to all for your help. I really appreciate your work and efforts.

Best,

Vincent

On Mon, Apr 19, 2010 at 11:21 AM, hadley wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> If you do want to use position_dodge, you need to explicitly specify the width:

> p <- ggplot(dataforplot,aes(riskcategory,mean,colour=Number))
> p + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lower.bound,ymax=upper.bound), position =
> position_dodge(width = 0.4))

>> A couple of prefatory comments:
>> (1) Text strings such as Low # of BITS without enclosing quotes lead to
>> trouble,
>>       especially for people who use textConnection() to cut and paste data
>> into the
>>       R console. Firstly, # is a comment indicator; secondly, R is going to
>> try to read
>>       what you intend as a single character string as four, and complain
>> about
>>       the mismatch between the number of variable names and the number of
>>       distinct fields it read. (Fortunately, I saw that coming; others may
>> not have.)
>> (2) In a ggplot() command, you want the + to be at the end of a line rather
>> than at
>>      the beginning if you intend the second line of code to be a
>> continuation of the first;
>>      otherwise, ggplot2 interprets the first line as a complete statement
>>      and tries to parse it.
>> More comments on this below.
>>
>> I ended up copying and pasting the data to a file and editing the Number
>> category
>> before entering it into R. In the end, I went with Low and High as the
>> Number.
>>
>> Since riskcategory is integer rather than a factor, the simplest way to
>> generate a
>> 'dodge' is to add a small amount to the riskcategory corresponding to High
>> in the Number
>> factor; I used 0.2. More specifically,
>>
>> dataforplot$riskcategory <- dataforplot$riskcategory + rep(c(0, 0.2), each =
>> 6))
>> p <- ggplot(dataforplot,aes(riskcategory,mean,colour=Number))
>> p + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lower.bound,ymax=upper.bound))
>>
>> gives you the dodged CIs by riskcategory colored by Number, with Number as
>> the
>> title of the legend. If you prefer "# of BITS" as the legend title, then use
>> p + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=lower.bound,ymax=upper.bound)) +
>>       scale_colour_hue("# of BITS")
>>
>> Since I complained about the data format supplied, it's only fair that I
>> show you
>> a better way to help people help you, and that is to use dput() on your data
>> frame:
>>
>> dput(dataforplot)
>> structure(list(riskcategory = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1.2, 2.2, 3.2,
>> 4.2, 5.2, 6.2), mean = c(0.26, 0.27, 0.28, 0.17, 0.01, 0, 0.44,
>> 0.27, 0.2, 0.09, 0, 0), sd = c(0.13, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.01, 0,
>> 0.19, 0.1, 0.1, 0.08, 0.01, 0), lower.bound = c(0.063, 0.122,
>> 0.112, 0.0275, 0.000151, 7.14e-07, 0.101, 0.104, 0.0395, 0.00448,
>> 7.51e-06, 1.26e-08), upper.bound = c(0.54, 0.5, 0.49, 0.41, 0.04,
>> 0.01, 0.79, 0.49, 0.43, 0.33, 0.03, 0), Number = structure(c(2L,
>> 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("High",
>> "Low"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("riskcategory", "mean",
>> "sd", "lower.bound", "upper.bound", "Number"), row.names = c(NA,
>> -12L), class = "data.frame")
>>
>> It's even more helpful if you type in the name of your data object and then
>> copy the
>> dput output to it when copying it into your e-mail, e.g.,
>>
>> dataforplot <-  structure(list(riskcategory = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1.2, 2.2,
>> 3.2,

>> 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("High",
>> "Low"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("riskcategory", "mean",

>> -12L), class = "data.frame")
